intro: Capsicums include both sweet peppers and chillies: colourful, heat-loving members of the tomato and potato family. In their native climate they are perennial plants, but in Britain they are grown as tender annuals and are most reliable under glass or in a warm, sheltered position. Green peppers are edible but are still an immature stage; if left to ripen they change colour and, in many varieties, become sweeter or hotter and more deeply flavoured. That extra flavour comes at a cost, because ripe-coloured fruit take longer to develop and the plant produces fewer new peppers while they mature. The crop is therefore a balance between earlier, heavier green harvests and later, smaller harvests of fully coloured fruit.

Cauliflower is one of the most rewarding brassicas, but also one of the least forgiving. The curd is a tight mass of flower buds, and the plant has to make strong, uninterrupted growth before it will produce a worthwhile head. Poor soil, loose planting, drought, overcrowding or a check after transplanting can all lead to tiny button heads or blind plants.

Celery is a moisture-loving crop grown for crisp, strongly flavoured stems, and it is much easier to enjoy than to grow beautifully. Traditional trench celery is grown for winter flavour, but it demands deep preparation, regular watering and careful earthing-up to exclude light from the stems. Self-blanching celery is simpler because close planting and a dense canopy do much of the blanching work, although it is less hardy and usually best harvested before cold weather.

Celeriac, or turnip-rooted celery, is grown for its swollen stem-base rather than for crisp stalks. It brings a strong earthy celery flavour to soups, stews, salads and winter dishes, and stores well into spring if lifted and kept cool. Although it avoids much of the blanching and earthing-up work of celery, it is still a long-season crop that needs rich, moisture-retentive soil, steady watering in dry weather and a good start under cover. The roots are fibrous and shallow, so growth is checked badly on dry ground; heavy, well-composted soil suits it especially well. Most varieties are quite similar, but all need the whole season to make a good-sized root.
